clue.text: Position filled by conservative type – me, old opera star

indicators.note: a space that is filled by something has that something put inside it

blocks.note: a placing is a position, as in a race
an old-fashioned, stick-in-the-mud person is called a dodo
ME is an alternative spelling of MI, the third note of tonic sol-fa
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A fusty Tory steps into a role and announces himself as a veteran opera singer.
explanation.walkthrough: The position is split after its I so the filling sits inside it. 'Me' looks like the setter speaking, but ME is an accepted spelling of the sol-fa note usually written MI.
explanation.definitionFit: Plácido Domingo is the celebrated Spanish tenor, one of the Three Tenors, so he is an example of an opera star.

clue.text: Statue like that which inspired Ozymandias, or the Venus de Milo?

definitions.text: like that which inspired Ozymandias, or the Venus de Milo

blocks.note: first meaning: a sculpture of head and shoulders

blocks.clueFragment: like that which inspired Ozymandias, or the Venus de Milo
blocks.note: second meaning: broken, as the shattered statue in Shelley's poem and the armless Venus are

explanation.walkthrough: Shelley's 'Ozymandias' was inspired by a ruined statue, trunkless legs and a shattered face; the Venus de Milo has lost her arms. Both are broken, and the same word also names a sculpted head and shoulders.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a noun for a sculpted head and torso and an informal adjective meaning broken or ruined.

clue.text: Poster stolen from field – that was spiteful!

indicators.note: something stolen from a place is taken away, leaving the rest behind

blocks.note: an advertisement, a poster, shortened
a meadow is a grassy field

explanation.surface: Someone tears a poster down from a field and gets a catty response.
explanation.walkthrough: Take AD out of MEADOW. The exclamation mark makes the definition a remark said in reply to a bitchy comment.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'miaow' after a remark mocks it as catty, a jibe that the comment was spiteful and cat-like.

clue.text: Stuck-up of course, maiden left a medium sweet white wine

indicators.note: in a down entry, being stuck up means pushed upwards, so the letters read from the bottom

blocks.note: 'of course!' is a word of agreement
M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over
L is the abbreviation for left
taken as written
M is the abbreviation for medium, as on clothes labels

explanation.surface: A snobbish girl leaves behind a glass of semi-sweet white.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuck-up' looks like snobbery describing the maiden, but it sends the whole string upward. A maiden is a cricket over with no runs scored.
explanation.definitionFit: Malmsey is a rich fortified Madeira made from Malvasia grapes, so it is a kind of sweet wine from pale grapes.

clue.text: Divers kind to seals short of nourishment? The opposite

indicators.note: divers is an old word for various or several, so the letters take varied positions
to seal something is to close it in, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
someone underfed looks thin

explanation.surface: A scuba diver is gentle with seals that look underfed, or is it the other way round?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divers' looks like underwater swimmers but is the archaic adjective. The rearranged letters wrap round THIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacked on after a statement, the phrase is a sarcastic tag meaning the reverse of what was just said is true.

clue.text: Professor of History who had an office in the Lodge?

definitions.text: who had an office in the Lodge

blocks.note: first meaning: an expert, read cryptically as a master of the past

blocks.clueFragment: who had an office in the Lodge
blocks.note: second meaning: a Freemason who has served as head of a lodge

explanation.walkthrough: A Masonic lodge is headed by a Master, and one who has held the post keeps a title saying so. An expert is also called this, and a history professor is literally an expert on bygone times.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a thorough expert, and in Freemasonry it is the title of a former Worshipful Master of a lodge.

clue.text: Gold king put in the care of eccentric landlady with her clowns

indicators.note: eccentric means off-centre and odd, so these letters sit in an odd order
whatever is in someone's care is held within their keeping

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
R stands for Rex, Latin for king
taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, joining the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A royal hands his gold to a dotty landlady and her comic lodgers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' looks like a link but joins the two words into one batch of eleven letters to rearrange; the symbol for gold and the Latin king then go in after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Stan Laurel and Oliver Hardy were the famous slapstick comedy double act of early Hollywood film.

clue.text: Not quite make it to the anti-toxin counter at the local pharmacy?

definitions.text: Not quite make it to the anti-toxin counter at the local pharmacy

blocks.clueFragment: Not quite make it to the anti-toxin counter
blocks.note: surface reading: a poisoned shopper collapses before reaching the antidote
setter's reading: the pharmacy is a branch of the UK chain named after its founder, so the death happens inside that shop

explanation.walkthrough: Boots is the big British chain of high-street chemists. The idiom normally means to die still working, without retiring; here it is read literally as expiring inside the shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Collapsing fatally before reaching the antidote inside a branch of the chemist chain is a literal death in that store.

clue.text: Reactionary produces cuttings for reading about Lassie?

indicators.note: a reactionary wants to turn the clock back, so the letters go backwards
about means around, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: mowing a lawn produces grass cuttings
for and to both mean towards, as in a train for London
a scan is a quick reading

explanation.surface: A right-wing fogey collects newspaper clippings to read up on a famous film collie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lassie' wants to be the collie of the films; the question mark warns it is the Scots word for a girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Lassie is the Scottish word for a girl or young woman, so a lassie is a female native of Scotland.

clue.text: Please refer to letter

blocks.note: first meaning: the instruction used in cross-references
second meaning: the third letter of the alphabet, written out as a word

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a polite instruction pointing to a letter; in fact the letter is the alphabet's third, whose name this word is.
explanation.definitionFit: Books use this word to send readers to another page, and the name of the third alphabet character is written with these letters.

clue.text: Further work required to clear top layer?

indicators.note: clearing something away removes it, so these letters are taken out

blocks.note: OP is short for opus, a work
taken as written
a laying hen is a layer of eggs

explanation.surface: A builder warns that more digging will be needed to strip away the topsoil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top layer' reads as topsoil, but the two words work separately, and a layer is a bird that lays eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as an adverb meaning moreover or in addition, as in 'and then there's the cost', it adds a further point.

clue.text: Waits, perhaps, as 007 reports?

blocks.note: first meaning: the first name of the American singer-songwriter surnamed Waits
second meaning: split two and one, it completes the phrase for how James Bond reports to his boss, M

explanation.surface: A question of whether waiting about is how James Bond files his reports.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waits' looks like a verb but is the surname of Tom Waits, the American singer-songwriter; 'perhaps' marks him as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Waits is a gravel-voiced American singer-songwriter, so his first name is an instance of someone called Waits.

clue.text: Youth’s rise inspires old people’s pain

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so one piece is taken inside another

blocks.note: an ascent is a rise
dole is an archaic word for grief, the pain of people in olden days

explanation.surface: A young person's growth spurt gives the elderly aches and pains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old people's pain' looks like arthritis, but it means the pain spoken of long ago: DOLE, as in doleful.
explanation.definitionFit: A youth is a young person between childhood and adulthood, which is exactly what a teenager in that stage is called.

clue.text: Cryptic and cagy, not quite Leonardo’s last oil

definitions.text: Cryptic and cagy, not quite Leonardo’s last oil

indicators.note: not quite all of something means a little is missing from the end
the last of a word is its final letter only
something cryptic is mysterious and obscure, so the letters are scrambled out of their plain order

blocks.note: taken as written, losing its final letter
the final letter of the painter's name
taken as written

explanation.surface: An evasive answer about the oil Leonardo used last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cryptic' and 'cagy' both suit the painting's famously enigmatic smile, which is why they are chosen; 'oil' does double duty, as letters and as the kind of painting.
explanation.definitionFit: La Gioconda is the Italian title of the Mona Lisa, Leonardo da Vinci's famous oil painting on poplar panel.

clue.text: Who’s this, setting for exhibitions?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone asks who is standing in a display venue
setter's reading: the answer's first word is the four letters of the first word rearranged, and its second word, ground, says they have been crushed and mixed

explanation.surface: A visitor at an exhibition venue asks who someone is.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer describes its own wordplay: its first half is an anagram of the clue's first word, and its second half is the anagram indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: A showground is an open site where agricultural shows, fairs and exhibitions are staged, the setting for such events.

clue.text: Having a beard of a brown colour, shaving face

indicators.note: shaving the face takes off what is at the front, so the first letter goes

blocks.note: tawny is an orange-brown colour

explanation.surface: A man with a brown beard shaves it off his face, a contradiction in itself.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'beard' is botanical: the bristles on ears of barley and other grasses are called awns.
explanation.definitionFit: The bristly awns on barley or wheat are called the plant's beard, so a grass with them is described this way.

clue.text: Slow pieces later, with a grand opening

indicators.note: an opening is a gap, so something is slotted into a gap in the other piece

blocks.note: 'later!' is a casual goodbye, as is the Spanish adiós
taken as written
G is short for grand, a thousand

explanation.surface: A concert programme saves the slow movements for later, after a big opening number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Later' reads as an adverb of time, but it is the slang farewell 'see you later'. 'Grand opening' tempts as a phrase; it splits.
explanation.definitionFit: An adagio is a piece or movement of music played at a slow tempo, so several of them are slow pieces.

clue.text: Is trained at initiation in function of Pope

indicators.note: an initiation is a beginning, so only the opening letter is wanted
in places one thing within another

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of the word
sine is a trigonometric function

explanation.surface: A cleric is schooled at his induction into a papal function.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Function' looks like a ceremony, but it is the maths sense. 'Initiation' sounds like a rite, fitting the church surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Sistine means relating to Pope Sixtus, the pontiff who built the famous chapel, so it is an adjective meaning of that Pope.

clue.text: 1 per cent of Brazil’s real airlines sadly excluded from revamped national service

indicators.note: sadly suggests things gone wrong, so the letters can come in any order
what is excluded is shut out, so these letters are removed
to revamp is to renovate and rework, so the remaining letters are reshaped

blocks.note: taken as written, letters removed in any order
taken as written

explanation.surface: Brazil's state carriers are cut out of a revamped national service budget, all for a pittance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Real' looks like an adjective but is Brazil's currency. Remove A, I, R, L, I, N, E, S from the fifteen letters and rearrange the seven left.
explanation.definitionFit: The Brazilian real is divided into one hundred centavos, so one centavo is a hundredth part of that currency.

clue.text: Job initially denied by big boss

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so just the opening letter is used
something denied is refused entry, so it is kept out

blocks.note: the first letter of the name
jumbo means extra large

explanation.surface: A job applicant is turned down at the start by the head of the firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big boss' reads as one phrase; split it, and the boss is the raised centre of a shield, not a manager.
explanation.definitionFit: An umbo is the round raised knob at the centre of a shield, which is also called a boss in that sense.

clue.text: Leaders trading in Bay 144 a big plus?

indicators.note: trading means exchanging, so the front letters swap places

blocks.note: a creek is a small bay or inlet
a gross is twelve dozen

explanation.surface: Managers making deals in a harbour think a huge sum is a big bonus.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the C and G at the heads of CREEK and GROSS. The question mark admits that a plus sign is only shaped like this cross.
explanation.definitionFit: A Greek cross has four arms of equal length, exactly the shape of a plus sign drawn large.

clue.text: Intimidate one in van, caught with cases

indicators.note: the van is the front of an army, so only the leading letter is wanted
to case something is to enclose it, so these letters go round another

blocks.note: c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
the first letter of the word
W is the abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: A thug in a van, arrested with suitcases, bullies someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Van' looks like a vehicle, but the van is the front, short for vanguard.
explanation.definitionFit: To cow someone is to frighten them into submission, which is what it means to intimidate a person.

clue.text: My tally for the game unveiled

indicators.note: removing a veil strips the outer covering, so the outside letters go

blocks.note: the score is the running tally in a match

explanation.surface: Someone shows off their own points count for a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' looks like a possessive but is the exclamation of surprise. Cor is a British exclamation like 'gosh'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of surprise or amazement, interchangeable as an interjection like wow or gosh.

clue.text: Mad about point one’s taken to heart

indicators.note: the heart is the middle, so the letters come from the centre of the words

blocks.note: the middle letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone is angry that a comment about them was taken personally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad' reads as angry, but 'mad about' is the keen sense. The letters sit across the inner part of the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Being keen on or enthusiastic about something, as in 'she's really into jazz', is being mad about it.

clue.text: Maybe just taking Pop to Plough?

blocks.note: first meaning: abstaining from alcohol, perhaps drinking only fizzy pop
second meaning: the Plough constellation is also called the Wagon, so going to it is going on to it

explanation.walkthrough: Capital P twice is misleading: Pop looks like Dad and Plough like a farm task. Pop is a soft drink; the Plough is the star group also known as the Wagon or Charles's Wain.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means teetotal for now, so someone drinking only soft drinks fits; the Plough's alternative name supplies the literal reading.

clue.text: Make new receiver set higher up

indicators.note: in a down entry, whatever is set higher up comes earlier, so the order of the two parts is fixed

blocks.note: the ear receives sound
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Install a fresh telephone receiver, mounted higher on the wall.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'set higher up' puts the receiver above the abbreviation for new, so it is written first.
explanation.definitionFit: To make money, as in 'she makes a good salary', is to earn it through work.

clue.text: All our characters book for tour in Australia

indicators.note: every character of a short word is to be struck out, leaving whatever else surrounds it

blocks.note: for and a both mean per, as in five pounds a head
taken as written, losing three letters
Oz is the slang name for Australia

explanation.surface: Every one of us books a trip round Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All our characters' also defines the alphabet, but here it strips O, U and R from TOUR. An A to Z is a British street-map book.
explanation.definitionFit: The A–Z is a well-known British brand of city street atlas, so the name is used for that book.

clue.text: Study done for housing firm backs court, in which Capone wound up?

indicators.note: a housing holds something within it
what backs something stands behind it, so this string comes after

blocks.note: to court someone is to woo them
a den is a private study
over means finished, done
for and at are both used of a price, as in sold at a pound
Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A detective's study of a firm behind a court case, the one where Al Capone finally came unstuck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wound up' suggests Capone's court case ending; here it means where he ended up. The phrase is gangster slang for a coffin.
explanation.definitionFit: A wooden overcoat is underworld slang for a coffin, the box in which a dead gangster like Capone finished.
